guides.title: Friendswood / Zone 9b Microclimate & Frost-Date Master Profile
steps: Friendswood (Galveston/Harris County border, USDA Zone 9b) averages a last spring frost around February 15–22 and a first autumn freeze around December 5–15, giving ~295 frost-free growing days—split into two distinct prime vegetable seasons (Spring: Feb–May; Fall: Sep–Dec) separated by an intense 100-day humid heatwave (Jun–Aug).

Manage the 3 local soil & climate realities: (1) heavy alkaline Beaumont/Lake Charles gumbo clay (pH 7.2–8.0) that holds standing water after 4-inch Gulf downpours; (2) 75%–95% coastal humidity driving early blight and powdery mildew; and (3) warm 76°F+ summer nights that halt tomato/pepper pollination.
Place a wireless dual-probe thermometer/hygrometer inside your greenhouse and garden to track night lows and daytime humidity spikes.
guides.safety: Always keep freeze cloth and pipe covers staged by November 15—Gulf Coast blue northers can drop temperatures from 78°F to 24°F in 12 hours.

guides.title: Backyard Greenhouse Orientation, Anchoring & Hurricane Wind Tie-Downs
steps: Orient your greenhouse ridge East-to-West in Friendswood so the long south-facing wall captures maximum low-angle winter sun from November through February.
Choose twin-wall polycarbonate panels (6mm–8mm) over single-layer glass or thin film—twin-wall channels trap insulating air for winter freezes AND diffuse harsh Texas sunlight to reduce leaf scorch.

Hurricane Anchoring (Mandatory on the Gulf Coast): Bolt the aluminum frame onto a heavy 4x4 timber perimeter sill anchored into the ground with 18-inch spiral earth augers at every corner, and seal polycarbonate panels into channels with neutral-cure silicone so 80+ mph gusts cannot pop panels out.
guides.safety: Before a named hurricane makes landfall, latch all roof vents shut (or remove lightweight vents) so wind cannot pressurize and lift the roof.

guides.title: Greenhouse Summer Cooling: Exhaust Fans, Shade Cloth & Evaporative Pads
steps: A closed Friendswood greenhouse hits 130°F+ by April—size your exhaust fan to exchange the entire air volume of the greenhouse once every 1 to 2 minutes (Length x Width x Avg Height = total CFM needed) with intake louvers on the opposite lower wall.

Drape 40%–50% Aluminet reflective shade cloth OVER THE EXTERIOR roof from May through September—blocking sunlight outside the roof drops interior temps by 12°F–18°F (hanging shade cloth inside still traps solar heat).
Install wax-cylinder automatic roof vent openers (require zero electricity) that push roof vents open automatically at 70°F and close at 60°F.
guides.safety: Keep interior oscillating fans running 24/7 even in summer to prevent stagnant humid fungal outbreaks.

guides.title: Greenhouse Winter Heating: Thermal Mass Barrels & Thermostat Heaters
gear: 1500W IPX4 waterproof greenhouse space heater with digital thermostat
steps: Line the north interior wall of your greenhouse with black-painted 55-gallon water barrels—water absorbs daytime solar heat and radiates steady warmth all night without electricity.
Insulate the north wall and lower knee-walls with large-bubble greenhouse bubble wrap (mist glass/polycarbonate with water and press flat side on—clings via static without tape).
Set a waterproof electric greenhouse heater with a built-in thermostat to kick on at 42°F–45°F for tropical citrus, orchids, and winter seedlings.
guides.safety: Use ONLY IPX4 splash-proof heaters rated for damp greenhouses plugged directly into a dedicated GFCI outlet—never household indoor heaters or extension cords.

guides.title: Greenhouse Seed-Starting Timeline for Friendswood (Spring & Fall Batches)
steps: Spring Batch (Start indoors/greenhouse Dec 26 – Jan 15): Sow tomatoes, sweet/hot peppers, eggplant, and basil on a 75°F–80°F heat mat so sturdy 8-inch transplants are ready to plant outdoors in Friendswood by February 20–March 1.
Early Cucurbits (Start Feb 1 – Feb 15 in biodegradable pots): Sow cucumbers, zucchini, cantaloupe, and watermelon 3 weeks before outdoor planting so they beat May squash vine borers.

Fall Batch (Start in shaded cool greenhouse Jul 15 – Aug 1): Sow fall tomatoes, broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, and kale under 50% shade cloth so tender seedlings survive August heat for September transplanting.
guides.safety: Keep a clean footbath mat or dedicated greenhouse shoes to avoid tracking outdoor soil-borne spider mites and whiteflies into your greenhouse.

guides.title: Greenhouse Pest & Humidity Control (Whiteflies, Spider Mites & Fungus Gnats)
steps: Fungus Gnats (from warm damp potting trays): Soak 2 tablespoons of Mosquito Bits (BTI) in 1 gallon of watering-can water for 30 minutes, strain, and drench seedling trays—kills gnat larvae within 48 hours without chemicals.

Spider Mites & Whiteflies (thrive in dry/warm greenhouse air): Mist plant undersides weekly with water, hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor early outbreaks, and spray insecticidal soap at dusk.
Quarantine any newly purchased nursery plant outside the greenhouse for 10 days before bringing it inside.
guides.safety: Never use sulfur burners inside polycarbonate greenhouses—sulfur vapor degrades polycarbonate panels and rusts aluminum frames.

guides.title: Top 12 Proven Vegetable & Fruit Varieties for Friendswood / Galveston County
supplies: Texas A&M AgriLife / Galveston County Master Gardener recommended seeds
steps: Tomatoes: Celebrity (determinate, disease-resistant), Solar Fire & Phoenix (sets fruit in 90°F+ heat), Sungold & Juliette (crack-resistant cherries).
Peppers: Jalapeño M, TAM Mild Jalapeño, Poblano/Ancho, Shishito, Tabasco, and Sweet Banana.
Greens & Brassicas: Lacinato (Dinosaur) Kale, Georgia Southern Collards, Redbor Kale, Malabar Spinach (summer vine), and Swiss Chard (Bright Lights).

Root & Summer Staples: Clemson Spineless Okra, Texas 1015Y Sweet Onions (plant sets in January), Beauregard Sweet Potatoes, Contender Bush Beans, and Celeste or Brown Turkey Figs + Owari Satsuma Mandarin.
guides.safety: Look for 'VFN' or 'VFFNTA' disease-resistance codes on tomato seed packets to resist Gulf Coast root-knot nematodes and Fusarium wilt.

guides.title: Fixing Alkaline Clay Nutrient Lockup (Iron Chlorosis & Blossom-End Rot)
supplies: Chelated Iron (EDDHA — specifically for high pH)
steps: Yellow leaves with dark green veins on citrus, blueberries, gardenias, and tomatoes in Friendswood indicate iron chlorosis caused by alkaline soil (pH >7.2) locking up iron.

Apply EDDHA-chelated iron (the ONLY iron chelate that stays soluble above pH 7.2) as a root drench for fast green-up within 10 days, and work elemental sulfur + pine bark fines into soil for gradual long-term pH lowering.
For tomato/pepper Blossom-End Rot (dark leathery bottom spots): add gypsum (provides calcium without raising pH like lime does) and keep soil moisture steady with mulch and drip lines.
guides.safety: Avoid agricultural lime in Friendswood soils unless a soil test proves pH is below 6.0—our native clay is already alkaline.

guides.title: Solarizing Beds in July–August to Wipe Out Nematodes & Bermuda Grass
supplies: Clear 2-mil to 4-mil UV-resistant polyethylene plastic sheet (NOT black plastic)
steps: In mid-July, clear weeds from an empty garden bed, rake smooth, and soak the soil deeply with water (wet soil conducts lethal solar heat far deeper than dry soil).

Stretch CLEAR plastic tightly over the damp bed and bury all 4 edges in a 4-inch trench so superheated air cannot escape—clear plastic acts like a greenhouse trapping 130°F–150°F heat down 6 inches deep, killing root-knot nematodes, fungal wilt, and Bermuda grass rhizomes.
Leave sealed for 6 weeks through August, remove plastic, and plant fall tomatoes or brassicas directly without deep tilling.
guides.safety: Use CLEAR plastic rather than black plastic—black plastic absorbs heat at the surface instead of heating the soil underneath.

guides.title: Overwintering Tropicals, Citrus & Orchids in a Friendswood Greenhouse
steps: In late November before the first cold front, hose off outdoor potted citrus, hibiscus, plumeria, bougainvillea, and orchids and spray undersides of leaves with horticultural oil so you don't bring scale or mealybugs indoors.
Stop fertilizing overwintered plants from November through January so they rest semi-dormant rather than pushing tender frost-sensitive new growth.
Water sparingly (only when top 2 inches of potting mix dry out) until bright warm February days return.
guides.safety: Acclimate greenhouse-wintered plants back to full outdoor sun gradually over 7–10 days in March so leaves don't sunburn.

guides.title: Greenhouse Watering Automation: Overhead Misters vs. Drip Lines
supplies: Inline pressure regulator (25 PSI) & mesh filter
steps: Use fine overhead micro-misters ONLY for germinating seedling flats and raising humidity for tropicals/orchids in the morning.
Run 1/4-inch drip emitters directly to the base of potted tomatoes, peppers, and citrus inside the greenhouse so leaves stay dry and free of gray mold (Botrytis) and powdery mildew.
Schedule watering for 7:00 AM–8:00 AM so excess moisture evaporates before evening.
guides.safety: Install a 25 PSI pressure regulator on city water spigots so high Friendswood water pressure doesn't blow barbed drip fittings apart.

guides.title: Hand-Pollinating Greenhouse Tomatoes, Peppers, Squash & Citrus
gear: Electric toothbrush (pollinator trick!) or small artist paintbrush
steps: Inside a screened greenhouse without wind or bees, blossoms drop unpollinated unless you pollinate manually.

Tomatoes & Peppers (self-fertile buzz-pollinated flowers): Gently touch the back of an electric toothbrush to the flower stem for 2 seconds between 10 AM and 2 PM—the vibration releases a visible puff of pollen onto the stigma.

Squash, Melons & Cucumbers (separate male and female flowers): Pluck a male flower (thin straight stem), peel back petals, and dab its pollen-covered anther directly onto the center of the female flower (which has a tiny baby fruit behind the petals).
guides.safety: Pollinate squash and melon flowers in the morning before noon while blossoms are open and receptive.

guides.title: Greenhouse Soil & Container Potting Mix Recipe (No Compaction)
supplies: 40% coco coir or sphagnum peat moss
10% pine bark fines + slow-release organic fertilizer
steps: NEVER put native Friendswood clay soil into greenhouse pots or raised trays—clay turns into airless mud in containers and suffocates roots.
Mix 4 parts coco coir/peat, 3 parts finished compost/worm castings, 2 parts coarse perlite, and 1 part pine bark fines for fast drainage with high nutrient holding.
Sterilize and reuse old container soil between seasons by solarizing in black bags in summer sun and re-amending with 25% fresh worm castings.
guides.safety: Wear a dust mask when pouring dry perlite or peat moss.

guides.title: Growing Avocados, Mangoes & Dragon Fruit in Friendswood Containers
supplies: Cold-hardy Mexican-race avocado (Lila, Joey, Fantastic, Poncho)
steps: Choose cold-hardy Mexican avocado cultivars ('Lila', 'Joey', or 'Fantastic'—hardy down to 18°F–20°F once mature) grafted onto rootstock, planted in ultra-fast-draining sandy/bark mound mix (avocados die rapidly in wet Friendswood clay).
Grow dwarf mangoes and dragon fruit in large wheeled containers so you can roll them straight into your heated greenhouse whenever winter forecasts drop below 32°F.
guides.safety: Avocado leaves, bark, and pits contain persin—keep pruned branches away from pets and livestock.

guides.title: Texas 1015Y Sweet Onions & Shallots (January Planting Guide)
supplies: Texas 1015Y Super Sweet onion transplant bundles (short-day variety!)
Ammonium sulfate or blood meal (high nitrogen)
steps: Plant ONLY 'Short-Day' onion varieties (Texas 1015Y, Red Creole, Yellow Granex) in Southeast Texas—long-day northern onions will never bulb at our latitude.

Plant pencil-thick transplants in mid-January 1 inch deep and 4–6 inches apart, and feed every 3 weeks with nitrogen until bulbs begin swelling in April (each leaf ring equals one onion layer—more leaves = bigger onions!).
Stop watering when tops fall over in May, pull bulbs, cure in shade for 2 weeks, and enjoy sweet onions all summer.
guides.safety: Discard any onion plants that send up a thick central flower stalk ('bolting')—use those immediately in the kitchen as they won't store.

guides.title: Beating Gulf Coast Early Blight, Powdery Mildew & Blossom Drop
supplies: Liquid copper fungicide or potassium bicarbonate
steps: Early Blight (brown bull's-eye spots on lower tomato leaves in humid May/June): Mulch bare soil 3 inches thick, strip bottom 12 inches of leaves, water strictly at the base, and spray copper fungicide or biofungicide (Serenade) early.
Powdery Mildew (white talcum dust on squash/cucumber leaves): Spray 1 tbsp potassium bicarbonate + 1/2 tsp Castile soap in 1 quart water at dusk, and plant mildew-resistant cultivars.
Summer Blossom Drop: When daytime temps top 92°F and nights stay above 75°F, tomato pollen clumps—install 30% shade cloth and switch to cherry/heat-set tomatoes until August fall planting.
guides.safety: Disinfect pruners with 70% alcohol after trimming blighted leaves so you don't carry spores to healthy plants.

guides.title: Gulf Coast Lawn & Yard Border Defense Against Bermuda Grass
supplies: 8-inch-deep steel or heavy HDPE root barrier edging
steps: Coastal Bermuda grass sends underground rhizomes 6 inches deep and 3 feet sideways into raised garden beds.
Dig a narrow 8-inch trench around garden perimeters with a drain spade and sink rigid steel or heavy-duty 60-mil HDPE edging leaving 2 inches protruding above soil.
Layer overlapping cardboard + 4 inches of arborist wood-chip mulch across all garden walkways so mowers never throw weed seeds into beds.
guides.safety: Call 811 before digging trenches deeper than 6 inches near utility easements.

guides.title: Hydroponic Kratky Lettuce & Herb Tubs Inside a Greenhouse
supplies: MasterBlend 4-18-38 + Calcium Nitrate + Epsom Salt hydroponic nutrients
steps: Zero-electricity Kratky Hydroponics: Cut 2-inch holes in an opaque tote lid, insert sprouted lettuce/basil/bok choy in rockwool net cups, and fill tote with nutrient solution (pH 5.8–6.2) touching ONLY the bottom 1/4-inch of the net cup.
As plants drink water over 4 weeks, the water level drops and leaves an air gap for upper oxygen roots—growing crisp salad heads in 28 days with zero pumps or timers.
guides.safety: Use opaque dark totes (or wrap mason jars in foil/socks) so sunlight cannot enter the nutrient water and grow green algae.

guides.title: Mosquito-Proofing Rain Barrels, Saucers & Yard Drainage in Friendswood
steps: In warm Friendswood weather, Aedes and Culex mosquitoes go from egg to biting adult in just 7 days in a bottlecap of standing water.

Drop 1/4 of a BTI Mosquito Dunk into every rain barrel, birdbath, and greenhouse water reservoir every 30 days—BTI is a naturally occurring soil bacterium harmless to humans, cats, dogs, birds, bees, and vegetable plants, killing ONLY mosquito and fungus-gnat larvae.
Empty plastic pot saucers after every rainstorm and keep French drains/swales clear of leaf dams.
guides.safety: BTI is completely non-toxic to pets and pollinators, unlike broad-spectrum yard fogging sprays that kill butterflies and bees.

guides.title: End-of-Season Greenhouse Deep Clean & Solar Sanitization
gear: Soft car-wash brush on extension pole
steps: In late July/August (peak Texas heat when outdoor gardening pauses), empty the greenhouse, scrub algae and dust off polycarbonate panels inside and out with mild soapy water and a soft brush (maximizes winter light transmission by 20%+).

Sanitize benches, pots, and trays with 3% hydrogen peroxide or 1:10 vinegar spray, then close vents for 3 sunny afternoons so 140°F+ solar heat naturally sterilizes lingering spider mites and fungal spores before fall seed starting.
guides.safety: Never use abrasive scouring pads or ammonia window cleaners on UV-coated polycarbonate panels.
